title: Pachira aquatica

{{Short description|Species of tree}} {{Speciesbox | image = Flickr - archer10 (Dennis) - Guatemala-1376.jpg | image_caption = Foliage and flower, Guatemala | status = LC | status_system = IUCN3.1 | status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI) |author2=IUCN SSC Global Tree Specialist Group |date=2019 |title=''Pachira aquatica'' |article-number=e.T146783390A146783392 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2019-2.RLTS.T146783390A146783392.en |access-date=13 December 2022}} | genus = Pachira | species = aquatica | authority = [[Jean Baptiste Christophore Fusée Aublet|Aubl.]] | synonyms = ''Carolinea macrocarpa''
''Bombax macrocarpum''
''Pachira macrocarpa'' }} {{Confusing|date=April 2025|reason=the article should be about the scientific species ''P.aquatica'', not ''P.glabra''}} '''''Pachira aquatica''''' is a [[species]] of tropical wetland tree in the mallow family [[Malvaceae]], native to [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]] where it grows in swamps. It is known by its common names '''Malabar chestnut''', '''French peanut''', '''Guiana chestnut''', '''provision tree''', '''Saba nut''', '''Monguba''' ([[Brazil]]), '''Pumpo''' ([[Guatemala]]) and '''Jelinjoche''' ([[Costa Rica]]) and is commercially sold under the names '''money tree''' and '''money plant'''. This tree is sometimes sold with a braided trunk and is commonly grown as a [[houseplant]], although more commonly what is sold as a "''Pachira aquatica''" houseplant is in fact a similar species, ''[[Pachira glabra]]''.[http://www.hawaiiantropicalplants.com/fruit.html "Pachira aquatica"] ''Hawaiian Tropical Plants Nursery'' ==Description== [[File:Pachira aquatica Tree.jpg|thumb|Cultivated tree]] ''Pachira aquatica'' can grow up to {{cvt|23|m}} tall with a diameter of {{cvt|70|cm}} at breast height.{{cite book |last1=Croat |first1=Thomas B. |author-link1=Thomas Croat |date=1978 |title=Flora of Barro Colorado Island |url=https://archive.org/details/floraofbarrocolo0000croa/page/589 |url-access=registration |language=en |edition=First |location=Stanford, California |publisher=Stanford University Press |pages=589–591 |isbn=978-0-8047-0950-7 |access-date=1 October 2024}} It has shiny green [[leaf shape|palmate]] leaves with [[lanceolate]] leaflets up to {{cvt|30|cm}} in length, and smooth green [[Bark (botany)|bark]]. This species forms a slightly thickened root with smaller roots, which also serves as a water [[reservoir]]. The relatively smooth [[bark (botany)|bark]] is brown through gray and slightly cracked; young branches are green. Outdoors, ''P. aquatica'' produces a broad crown. The transitional and long-[[stalked]], composite hand-shaped, slightly leathery leaves are arranged at the branch ends. The [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] is up to {{cvt|24|cm}} long. The leaves are bright green and shiny and consist of up to nine leaflets (fingers). The mostly glabrous, short-stalked leaflets are up through 28 cm long and rounded through round pointed, spiked, or pointed. They are [[lanceolate]] or obovate, with a light middle veins. There are sloping [[stipule]]s present. The leaves and flowers are also often eaten.{{cite journal |last1=Oliveira |first1=J.T.A |last2=Vasconcelos |first2=I.M |last3=Bezerra |first3=L.C.N.M |last4=Silveira |first4=S.B |last5=Monteiro |first5=A.C.O |last6=Moreira |first6=R.A |title=Composition and nutritional properties of seeds from Pachira aquatica Aubl, Sterculia striata St Hil et Naud and Terminalia catappa Linn |journal=Food Chemistry |date=August 2000 |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=185–191 |doi=10.1016/S0308-8146(00)00076-5 }}{{Cite journal |last1=Rodrigues |first1=Alexsandra Pereira |last2=Pastore |first2=Glaucia Maria |date=2021-06-01 |title=A review of the nutritional composition and current applications of monguba (Pachira aquatica Aubl.) plant |journal=Journal of Food Composition and Analysis |language=en |volume=99 |article-number=103878 |doi=10.1016/j.jfca.2021.103878 |issn=0889-1575|doi-access=free }} Its showy flowers, said to have the fragrance of lilacs,{{cite book |last=Zuchowski |first=Willow |title=Tropical Plants of Costa Rica |date=2007 |publisher=Cornell Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-8014-4588-0 |location=Ithaca, N.Y. |page=252}} have long, narrow [[petal]]s up to {{cvt|32|cm}} long, that open like a banana peel to reveal hairlike yellowish orange [[stamen]]s. The greenish-yellow or cream-colored, [[hermaphroditic]] and very large, short and thick-stalked flowers with double [[perianth]] resemble shaving brushes through the long [[stamens]]. The terminal, single, twofold, or threefold flowers suggest that [[bat]]s are the [[pollinator]]s. The outside fine-haired, green-brown and overgrown [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] is cup-shaped and about 2 cm long. The narrow, elongated petals can reach up to 30 cm long. Flowers with petals up to {{cvt|34|cm}} long and {{cvt|5.5|cm}} wide have been reported on [[Barro Colorado Island]]. The approximately 180–250 stamens, deep pink at the top and yellow at the base,{{cite book | last= Rohwer | first= Dr. Jens G. | date= 2002 | title= Tropical Plants of the World | location= New York | publisher= Sterling Pub. Co. Inc. | pages= 80 plus photo p. 81 | isbn= 0-8069-8387-6}} with elongated anthers are overgrown and tufted above. The five-chambered [[Ovary (botany)|ovaries]] uppermost with a long stylus with divided, short lobed scar. The capsules are large, brown, woody, up to 20–30 cm long, rough, and egg-shaped, with a diameter of about 10–15 cm, weigh about 1–1.5 kg, and contain 10–25 nuts.{{cite book | last= Croat | first= Thomas B. | date= 1978| title= Flora of Barro Colorado Island| location= Stanford, Calif. |publisher= Stanford Univ. Press | pages= 589–591}} ==Etymology== The genus name is derived from a language spoken in [[Guyana]].Helmut Genaust (1983): Etymologisches Wörterbuch der botanischen Pflanzennamen, 2. Auflage. Birkhäuser Verlag – {{ISBN|3-7643-1399-4}} The species name is [[Latin]] for "aquatic". It is classified in the subfamily [[Bombacoideae]] of the family [[Malvaceae]]. Previously it was assigned to [[Bombacaceae]].[http://ara.inbio.ac.cr/SSTN-IABIN/species/154777 IABIN] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120701113001/http://ara.inbio.ac.cr/SSTN-IABIN/species/154777|date=2012-07-01}}{{cite web |author=John H. Wiersema |title=GRIN |url=http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/genus.pl?8717 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121010064327/http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/genus.pl?8717 |archive-date=2012-10-10 |access-date=2012-01-27 |publisher=Ars-grin.gov}} The name "money tree" is believed to refer to a story of its origin, in which a poor man prayed for money, found this "odd" plant, took it home as an omen, and made money selling plants grown from its seeds.{{cite web |title=Money Tree Bonsai, Wedding Favors, Corporate Gifts, Plant Gifts |url=http://www.natureperfect.com/shop/money_tree_bonsai.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115043855/http://www.natureperfect.com/shop/money_tree_bonsai.html |archive-date=2012-01-15 |access-date=2012-01-27 |publisher=Natureperfect.com}} ==Cultivation== {{Multiple image | direction = vertical | image1 = Pachira aquatica (fruit) edit1.jpg | image1_size = 100px | image2 = Pachira aquatica (inflorescense).jpg | image2_size = 100px | footer = ''P. aquatica'' fruit and flower }} Most trees cultivated as [[ornamental plant|ornamental]] houseplants that are identified as ''Pachira aquatica'' are actually the related ''[[Pachira glabra]]''. While both ''P. aquatica'' and ''P. glabra'' have such ornamental uses,Lothar Staeck. ''Fascination Amazon River: Its People, Its Animals, Its Plants''. Springer-Verlag, 2022. [https://books.google.com/books?id=xiZcEAAAQBAJ&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&lpg=PP1&pg=PA116#v=onepage&q&f=false p. 116.] {{ISBN|9783662644522}} the often-braided houseplant known as a "money tree" originally exported from Taiwan is ''P. glabra''. The association with ''P. aquatica'' derives from an early misidentification in Taiwan. As plant author Wang Jui-minChen Pei-ying. "一株蝴蝶蘭緣何飛過大海：專訪《福爾摩沙雨林植物誌》胖胖樹王瑞閔 [How a Phalaenopsis Orchid Flies Across the Ocean: An Interview with Pangpang Shu Wang Jui-min, the Fat Tree Author of ''Flora of the Formosa Rainforest'']". ''[[Central News Agency (Taiwan)|Central News Agency]]''. 19 August 2018. Retrieved 20 March 2025. explains that "for a long time, [this plant] was mistakenly believed to be the ''Pachira aquatica'' widely distributed in Central and South America...Later it was discovered that the filaments of the Malabar chestnut are red and the fruit is covered with reddish-brown hairs, which is significantly different from the smooth chestnut commonly cultivated in Taiwan". He notes that "all species cultivated in Taiwan are ''Pachira glabra''". The tree grows well as a tropical ornamental in moist, frost-free areas, and can be started from seed or [[cuttings (plant)|cutting]]. It is a durable plant and adapts well to different conditions. The plant requires bright light, but not direct sunlight. When grown indoors it requires a very gradual introduction to direct sunlight outdoors to reduce the chances of sunburning its leaves. This tree thrives in both common [[potting soil]] and water in a [[hydroponic]] system. The plant grows well in bright light, but also tolerates partial shade at room temperatures from 12 °C through 25 °C. A plant's leaves may turn yellow and fall when days are shorter in autumn which is not a sign of disease, and the plant will restart its growth without problem the following spring. A tree is mature when 4–5 years old. It produces its first fruit in spring and fall. Furthermore, it can withstand temperatures as low as 5 °C without losing its leaves, although people recommended not growing it below 12 °C as an orangery tree, the ideal culture temperature being about 20 °C all year round with high humidity. An occasional weak [[frost]] can cause it to lose its leaves, and it grows new leaves in the following spring.Jules Janick, Robert E. Paull: The Encyclopaedia of Fruit and Nuts. CABI, 2008, {{ISBN|978-0-85199-638-7}}, p. 182 et seq. This species is occasionally cultivated for its [[Nut (fruit)|nuts]], which grow in a large, woody [[capsule (botany)|capsule]].Food and fruit-bearing forest species. 3: Examples from Latin America, FAO Forestry Paper 44/3, FAO 1986, {{ISBN|92-5-102372-7}}, p. 213 et seq. The nuts are light brown, striped with white, about 2–3 cm long, and embedded in a spongy and fibrous [[pericarp]]. The capsule is not eaten. The nuts develop within until the capsule bursts and releases them. The nuts are considered edible, with a flavor similar to a European chestnut. Some people grind the nuts and use them in a hot drink. They are toxic to rats in the raw state, but are consumed by people raw or roasted.{{cite book|last=Duarte|first=Odilo|author2=Robert E. Paull|title=The Encyclopedia of Fruit and Nuts|year=2006|publisher=CABI|location=Cambridge, MA|isbn=978-0-85199-638-7|pages=182–183|editor=Jules Janick, Robert Paull|chapter=Pachira aquatica: Malabar chestnut}} ==Potential health risks== The presence of cyclopropenoid [[fatty acid]]s (CPFAs) in the nuts has been used to state that the nuts are not edible and not suitable for human consumption, despite the nut being eaten or used in medicine. At least one review indicates that CPFAs are [[carcinogen]]ic, [[co-carcinogen]]ic, and have medical and other effects on animals;{{cite journal |last1=Hanus |first1=Lumir Ondrej |last2=Goldshlag |first2=Paulina |last3=Dembitsky |first3=Valery Mikhail |title=Identification of cyclopropyl fatty acids in walnut (Juglans regia L.) oil |journal=Biomedical Papers |date=1 June 2008 |volume=152 |issue=1 |pages=41–45 |doi=10.5507/bp.2008.006 |pmid=18795073 |doi-access=free }} according to this review, "CPFA in food is dangerous to human health". Out of six rats tested in a study of ''P. aquatica'', five died after consuming the nuts. The surviving rat had enlarged organs including the stomach, liver, pancreas, kidneys, lungs and also had spleen atrophy. Research on the health effects of eating the nuts on humans is lacking, but there are some studies regarding nutritional facts and food utilization.{{cite journal |last1=Jorge |first1=Neuza |last2=Luzia |first2=Débora Maria Moreno |title=Caracterização do óleo das sementes de Pachira aquatica Aublet para aproveitamento alimentar |journal=Acta Amazonica |date=March 2012 |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=149–156 |doi=10.1590/S0044-59672012000100017 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2012AcAma..42..149J |hdl=11449/30867 |hdl-access=free }}{{cite journal |last1=Silva |first1=Bernadete De Lourdes De Araújo |last2=Azevedo |first2=Claudia Carneiro De |last3=Azevedo |first3=Fátima De Lourdes Assunção Araújo |title=Propriedades funcionais das proteínas de amêndoas da munguba (Pachira aquatica Aubl.) |trans-title=Functional properties of proteins from almonds of the guiana-chestnut (Pachira aquatica aubl.) |language=pt |journal=Revista Brasileira de Fruticultura |date=March 2015 |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=193–200 |doi=10.1590/0100-2945-065/14 |doi-access=free }}{{cite journal |last1=Silva |first1=A.
